intro: Four buildings invite the body to follow four different routes.
alt: Four entrances show curved masonry, a ceremonial stair, a glass volume and timber ledges in woodland.

variants.name: Baroque architecture
variants.look: Curved masonry guides the eye around the approach and into deep shadow.
variants.history: Seventeenth-century Baroque designers in Rome used curved plans, dramatic light and rhythmic architectural forms.
variants.when: Make entry dynamic by changing what is visible with each step.
variants.why: Curvature and alternating light change the appearance of the approach as you move.

variants.name: Beaux-Arts architecture
variants.look: The monumental stairs and matching wings pull the visitor toward a single threshold.
variants.history: Design training at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris emphasized formal composition, the architectural axis and classical precedent.
variants.when: Use grandeur and symmetry to turn an approach into a public ceremony.
variants.why: A centered axis and successive layers establish threshold and rank from a distance.

source.label: The Met · The Architecture of The Met

variants.name: International Style architecture
variants.look: Rectangular surfaces and glass dissolve some boundaries between interior and exterior.
variants.history: The International Style label was popularized by Henry-Russell Hitchcock and Philip Johnson in connection with MoMA’s 1932 architecture exhibition.
variants.when: Show the building as adjoining volumes with lightweight surfaces.
variants.why: Regular thin supports and transparent planes let the viewer compare interior and exterior at once.

variants.name: organic architecture
variants.look: Broad horizontal terraces and timber echo the rock ledges and trees.
variants.history: Frank Lloyd Wright developed his idea of organic architecture around the relationship among building, landscape, furnishings and inhabitants.
variants.when: Let the site suggest how rooms project, shelter and open.
variants.why: Materials and projecting planes echo the features and scale of the original landscape.
variants.period: Early to mid-20th century, with later practice

prompt: Draw a single textless art comparison board for a museum-quality online art atlas. Layout is exactly four square cells in 2x2, edge-to-edge, no gutters or borders; precise, strictly equally sized cells. Order is left to right within each row, then next row. Each cell is a distinct style treatment featuring the same female executive from reference, in original new art. The reference image is for identity only: recognizable ash-blonde hair in neat low bun with four-color windowpane hair clip, black-rimmed rectangular glasses over blue eyes, charcoal sheath dress under fitted black blazer, azure pocket square and blue lanyard with blank ID badge, holding a white coffee mug with a little four-color tile mark. Change the actual render style rather than adding only backgrounds. Layout styles in order: Baroque: convex and concave folds, shadowed colonnade, dramatic clouds and oval space; Beaux-Arts: monumental marble steps, heroic symmetry, pediment and carefully symmetrical axial entrance; International Style: sharp orthogonal glass volumes, narrow steel supports and outside/inside transparency; organic architecture: layered rock ledges and timber roof planes extending into a forest ravine. Each scene shows same executive holding mug as a human scale cue. No readable text, numbers, signatures, words, or extra panels.
